segments.say: Lesson 16. Trees 101. What a tree is, every key term (root, leaf, height. ), binary trees, B S Ts and how a TreeNode looks in Python.

A tree is a set of nodes connected like a family tree: one root at the top, each node can have children, and there are no loops. Here is an analogy. A company org chart: the C E O is the root, managers are internal nodes, and people with no reports are leaves. Your computer's folders work the same way.

Why does this matter? Tree questions are extremely common: traversal, depth, paths, B S T checks. Heaps, tries and many graph problems build on tree ideas. A few key words. Node: One element, holding a value and links to its children. Root: The top node, with no parent. Parent / child: A node directly above / below another. Leaf: A node with no children. Depth: How many edges from the root down to a node. Height: The longest path from a node down to a leaf. Binary tree: Each node has at most 2 children: left and right. B S T: Binary search tree: left subtree less than node less than right subtree.

segments.sec: Watch: Anatomy of a binary tree
segments.say: Anatomy of a binary tree. Every tree starts at the root (8). It's the only node without a parent.

segments.sec: Watch: Anatomy of a binary tree
segments.say: 8 has two children: 3 (left) and 10 (right). 8 is their parent. Lines between nodes are edges.

segments.sec: Watch: Anatomy of a binary tree
segments.say: Next level: 1 and 6 are children of 3; 14 is the right child of 10 (10 has no left child, and that's allowed).

segments.sec: Watch: Anatomy of a binary tree
segments.say: Nodes with no children are leaves: 1, 6, 14. The node 3 together with everything below it forms a subtree.

segments.sec: Watch: Anatomy of a binary tree
segments.say: Depth of node 1 equals 2 edges from the root. The tree's height equals 2 (the longest root-to-leaf path).

segments.sec: Watch: Anatomy of a binary tree
segments.say: It's a binary tree (at most 2 children each), and also a B S T: everything left of 8 is smaller, everything right is bigger. Same at every node.
Searching a B S T for 6. Find 6. Start at the root: is 6 less than 8? Yes, so it can only be in the left subtree. The whole right side is skipped.
At 3: is 6 less than 3? No, 6 greater than 3, so go right.
Found 6 in 3 steps. Each step drops half the tree (when balanced), so search is O of log n, the same idea as binary search.
The TreeNode class (used in every LeetCode tree problem). Here is the code. Pause the video to read it line by line.

Kinds of binary trees. Full: every node has 0 or 2 children. Complete: every level filled left to right (heaps are complete). Balanced: left and right heights differ by at most 1 everywhere, so height about log n. Skewed: basically a linked list, so height equals n and operations become O of n.

How you will process trees. D F S (depth-first, usually recursive): go deep into one branch before the next. Next lesson. B F S (breadth-first, with a queue): level by level. The lesson after. Almost every tree solution is: handle None, solve left, solve right, combine.

segments.sec: Problem 1: Search in a Binary Search Tree
segments.say: Problem 1: Search in a Binary Search Tree. Given the root of a B S T and a value, return the node holding that value (or None). For example, with root equals 4,2,7,1,3, val equals 2, the answer is node 2 (with children 1 and 3).

segments.sec: Problem 1: Search in a Binary Search Tree
segments.say: The obvious brute force: Visit every node (any traversal) until you find the value, ignoring the B S T ordering. That costs O of n time. The smart way: Use the B S T rule: smaller values are left, bigger values are right. Walk down one path only. Step by step: Start at the root. Then, If val less than node.val go left, if bigger go right. Then, Stop when you find it or hit None.
Here is the Python solution. Complexity: O of h time (log n if balanced), O of 1 space. Pause and read through it, then try writing it yourself without looking.
Problem 2: Same Tree. Return True if two binary trees have exactly the same shape and values. For example, with p equals 1,2,3, q equals 1,2,3, the answer is True.

The obvious brute force: Serialize both trees to lists (including Nones) and compare the lists. That costs O of n time, O of n extra space. The smart way: Recursion: two trees are the same if the roots match, the left subtrees are the same, and the right subtrees are the same. Step by step: Both None leads to True. Then, One None or different values leads to False. Then, Return same(left, left) and same(right, right).
Here is the Python solution. Complexity: O of n time, O of h stack. Pause and read through it, then try writing it yourself without looking.

Problem 3: Invert Binary Tree. Mirror a binary tree: swap the left and right children of every node. For example, with root equals 4,2,7,1,3,6,9, the answer is 4,7,2,9,6,3,1. Every left/right pair is swapped at every level

The obvious brute force: There's no slower obvious way here. You must touch every node once, so the question is just how to write it cleanly. That costs O of n is the minimum. The smart way: Recursion: invert the left subtree, invert the right subtree, then swap them. The base case is an empty node. Step by step: If node is None, return None. Then, Recursively invert both children. Then, Swap them and return the node.
Here is the Python solution. Complexity: O of n time, O of h stack. Pause and read through it, then try writing it yourself without looking.

A likely interview question: What makes a B S T useful? A strong answer: The ordering rule (left less than node less than right) means each comparison discards a whole subtree, so search, insert and delete take O of height, which is O of log n when balanced.
